issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is a highly specific trigger that is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type of police violence as described here. The other trigger, threat, memory, and strategy items all center on generalized danger/hypervigilance and perpetrator-related reminders, not exposure/undress themes. Without any corroborating memory or appraisal content about forced stripping, searches, or sexualized humiliation, this item looks clinically mismatched.

In this profile it appears disconnected from the identified trauma network and is hard to explain clinically as part of the same PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Claire Donovan was 31 when she came for treatment, a divorced White American woman who had spent most of her adult life in uniform herself, working as a paramedic. The event she circled back to again and again had happened after a late shift, on a night when she was already worn down and keyed up from work. She had been near her ambulance, still in her station clothes, when police approached during a chaotic scene. What she remembers most sharply is not a clean sequence but fragments that arrive with the force of the present: the abrupt nearness of a uniformed body, hands on her before she was ready, the shock of being grabbed, the sense that her own explanations did not matter once the encounter had turned physical. When she tries to tell it from beginning to end, she falters. She starts with one image, then jumps to another, then stops altogether, frustrated and embarrassed, saying she knows it sounds scattered but that the memory does not come in order. What is clearest to her is the feeling that she was no longer a fellow responder or a person who could speak for herself, but someone pinned inside a moment that could turn dangerous without warning.

In the weeks afterward, Claire found that reminders of the officer who hurt her seemed to gather everywhere. Police uniforms, badges, the stance and voice of authority, even the sight of someone taking control of a scene could make her body tense before she had fully registered why. At work this became especially hard. As a paramedic, she frequently arrived alongside police or entered scenes already controlled by them. She began hanging back when officers were present, letting her partner take the lead when possible, and keeping her speech clipped and purely functional. She told herself she was just staying professional, but privately she was doing everything she could to avoid anything that reminded her of the man who had put hands on her. Even outside work she steered away from authority figures in uniform, changing aisles in stores, leaving public places early, or declining events where security staff or police might be visible.

She had also come to believe that anger was dangerous and had to be shut down immediately. Any flicker of it felt unacceptable to her. If she noticed herself becoming angry about what had been done to her, she forced it down at once, tightening her jaw, changing the subject, telling herself to get over it. She never allowed herself to express it openly. Friends sometimes experienced her as flat or distant, and in the aftermath of her divorce she felt more isolated than she wanted to admit. She could describe being hurt, humiliated, and frightened more easily than she could admit fury. Anger, in her mind, was something that would make everything less controlled.

Her body now moved through the world as if danger might break through at any moment. In restaurants she never sat with her back to the room. In waiting areas she chose seats near exits or against walls where no one could come up behind her. On shift she was constantly aware of where everyone was standing, who was moving toward her, what was in their hands, whether a scene could change suddenly. She scanned doorways, voices, posture, the energy between people. She reacted sharply if anyone touched her unexpectedly. A colleague brushing past her in the ambulance bay or placing a hand on her shoulder without warning could make her jump hard enough to feel ashamed afterward. She knew other people did not understand why such small contact set off such a strong alarm, but for Claire the reaction was immediate and physical.

Stress seemed to lower the threshold for everything. After difficult calls, staffing shortages, or conflict on shift, she noticed nausea creeping in, sometimes so quickly that she had to step away and steady herself. In those moments the memory could press close in a way that did not feel like remembering. It felt current, as though the event were unfolding again in her body rather than residing in the past. She would lose her place mid-story when trying to explain this, trailing off because the details no longer lined up into something coherent enough to tell.

What finally brought Claire in was a recent incident at work. An officer at a scene touched her arm unexpectedly to move her aside, and she recoiled so abruptly that everyone noticed. Later she felt sick, rattled, and deeply exposed. She was frightened by how little control she seemed to have over her own reactions and by how much effort it now took to get through an ordinary shift. At the same time, she was hoping for something simple but urgent: to be able to work, sit in a room, and be approached by another person without feeling as if she had to brace for danger before she could breathe.
